source: Wilie, Cahyawijaya, Ishii, He, Fung (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of Large Language Models Reasoning (Belief-R)
finding: This is an LLM test built on the Byrne suppression design. Step t: two premises give a modus ponens or modus tollens conclusion. Step t+1: a third conditional is added. If it adds a requirement (p and r needed for q), the model should retract and say 'may or may not q' (Belief Update). If it adds an alternative route (r also leads to q), the model should keep the conclusion (Belief Maintain). Answers are three-way: q, not q, may or may not q. So the earlier premise that no LLM suppression study exists (K26) is wrong.
numbers: Dataset built from ATOMIC if-then events with GPT-4-series generation and a crowd-worker check. 1912 basic items at step t; 1074 Belief Update and 670 Belief Maintain items (1744 with three premises); modus ponens and modus tollens in equal shares for the update set (537 each). 30 LMs tested. BREU = mean of update accuracy and maintain accuracy.
limits: Third premises are LLM-generated and filtered by crowd workers; commonsense knowledge decides which type a third premise is, so knowledge and logic are mixed. Models: Llama-3 70B, Mixtral 8x22B, Command R/R+, Claude 3 Haiku/Sonnet, GPT-3.5/4 Turbo; no reasoning-tuned models.
agent_relevance: Direct test of the suppression pattern. The agent needs a rule: after a new premise, ask whether it is a requirement or an alternative before keeping or retracting.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief-R, results (Figure 4 and Table A1)
finding: LLMs almost never retract when they should (low Belief Update accuracy) while they keep the conclusion when they should (high Belief Maintain accuracy). They lean toward 'keep'. Chain-of-thought and plan-and-solve do not fix it: the mean BREU gain is about 1 point.
numbers: Direct / CoT / plan-and-solve, as Belief-Update acc / Belief-Maintain acc / BREU: Llama-3 70B Instruct 10.99/92.09/51.54, 12.57/89.40/50.99, 12.66/88.21/50.44. GPT-4 Turbo 19.65/82.69/51.17, 21.51/81.19/51.35, 16.76/83.73/50.25. Mixtral 8x22B direct 35.38/36.57/35.98, CoT 27.28/34.93/31.11, plan-and-solve 44.04/53.13/48.59. Claude 3 Sonnet direct 9.40/88.66/49.03. Text: best models reach at most about 50% BREU; most non-API models near 0% Belief Update.
limits: Table A1 rows for the last two models are unlabeled in the PDF text, so only named rows are cited. Maintain accuracy drops versus plain inference for most models when a distractor third premise is added (Appendix C.1, 378 matched items).
agent_relevance: A 'list defeaters first' step is a different prompt from CoT or plan-and-solve and is untested here. These results say plain CoT is not enough. Test: classify the added premise as requirement or alternative as an explicit state, scored on the update and maintain subsets at equal tokens.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief-R, modus ponens versus modus tollens and effect type
finding: Belief revision is harder with modus tollens bases: BREU is lower, with higher update accuracy but much lower maintain accuracy than for modus ponens. The authors tie this to backward reasoning and negation. Models also tend to keep their belief when the added premise concerns mental-state effects (abstract) rather than events.
numbers: Only described in the text (Figures 5a and 5b); no exact per-condition values extracted. Mental-state items: 504 basic, 276 update; event items: 1408 basic, 798 update.
limits: The explanation (backward reasoning, negation) is the authors' reading and was not tested.
agent_relevance: Supports putting a contrapositive or negation-check step on modus tollens items. Not yet shown to work.

source: Chan, Gaizauskas, Zhao (2025) RULEBREAKERS: Challenging LLMs at the Crossroads between Formal Logic and Human-like Reasoning (ICML)
finding: The opposite failure to suppression. For modus tollens and disjunctive syllogism items where world knowledge says the formally valid conclusion should be rejected (for example 'Anne is in Stockholm or Sweden; she is not in Sweden'), models still accept it. They apply the rule too rigidly. Models do better on disjunctive syllogism than on modus tollens.
numbers: Seven LLMs. Only Llama-3-8B-Instruct has paired accuracy above 0.6 (chance baseline 0.25). GPT-4o and Gemma-2-27b-it score perfectly on non-rulebreakers but worst on rulebreakers. GPT-4o paired accuracy 0.0022 on the modus tollens categorical-entity subset. Models are more confident in 'yes' for non-rulebreakers than for rulebreakers (p < 0.0001), so some latent signal exists.
limits: Models up to GPT-4o and Gemma-2; no reasoning-tuned models. Paired accuracy needs both prompts right, which is strict. Rulebreakers differ from Byrne suppression but use the same cue: a premise the reasoner knows undermines the rule.
agent_relevance: Argues against a pure formal-solver front end for natural-language conditionals. Check a formally valid conclusion against world knowledge before accepting it. Test items can be generated cheaply.

source: Orth, Mondorf, Plank (2026, EACL) If Probable, Then Acceptable? Understanding Conditional Acceptability Judgments in Large Language Models
finding: First LLM study of the Equation (acceptability of 'if A then B' tracks P(B|A)) with the relevance manipulation of Skovgaard-Olsen et al. 2016. Models gave 0-100 ratings for three tasks: P(B|A) from a split 'Suppose A. B?' format, the probability of the full conditional, and acceptability. All models respond to P(B|A). They also respond to relevance, but less consistently than people. The conjunction and material-conditional readings were not tested directly.
numbers: Llama 8B/70B and Qwen 7B/72B, vanilla, few-shot, and CoT (CoT only for the 70B and 72B). 144 conditionals (3 relation types x 4 prior levels x 12 contexts). Each prompt sampled 5 times at T = 1.0. Fixed-effect slope on P(B|A) for vanilla models, as read from Table 2 (the PDF table is partly scrambled): Llama 8B 0.35, Llama 70B 0.65, Qwen 7B 0.38, Qwen 72B 0.21. P(B|A) main effect p < 0.0001 for all models. Relation-type effect vs irrelevant (NEG / POS): Llama 8B 0.10 / 0.30, Llama 70B 0.07 / 0.01, Qwen 7B 0.06 / 0.26, Qwen 72B 0.20 / 0.30. Human reference data: Skovgaard-Olsen 2016.
limits: P(B|A) in the stimuli comes from human norming, not from the model, so this does not show that the model's own P(B|A) equals its P(if). Small open models only; the Table 2 row mapping is inferred from the layout. No frontier or reasoning models.
agent_relevance: The agent should not assume its own acceptability of a conditional equals its conditional probability, and should check relevance explicitly. A direct probe: ask the same model for P(C|A) and P(if A then C) on irrelevant-antecedent items and compare.

source: Orth et al. (2026), comparison with human data
finding: Human ratings give the cleanest relevance pattern: slopes on P(B|A) are steepest for positively related conditionals. LLMs differ. Larger models, few-shot and CoT variants show steeper slopes for negatively related than positive ones, the reverse of people. Llama 70B vanilla barely separates relation types. Smaller models integrate relevance more consistently than larger ones. Mean ratings for irrelevant and negative conditionals match humans; the gap is in the positive condition. Few-shot or CoT did not move models toward human behaviour.
numbers: Human means (centered -0.5 to 0.5): IRR -0.25, NEG -0.26, POS 0.19. LLM means range -0.37 to -0.20 (IRR) and -0.27 to -0.19 (NEG). Positive mean: Llama 8B 0.01, Llama 70B 0.04, Qwen 7B 0.06, Qwen 72B 0.16 (vanilla), 0.15 (few-shot), 0.14 (CoT). Llama 70B few-shot NEG-minus-POS slope difference 0.20 (p < .001). Relation-type effect absent for Llama 70B vanilla (p = 0.060).
limits: Comparison uses Skovgaard-Olsen et al. (2016) human data (N = 348 kept of 577, slopes .78 / .61 / .43), which I did not re-derive here.
agent_relevance: The Equation check (K14, K15) holds in direction for LLMs but not in shape. A relevance check step may be needed before accepting a conditional.

source: Orth et al. (2026), repeated-sample consistency
finding: Each prompt was sampled five times at temperature 1.0. Numeric ratings are fairly reproducible for large models and less so for the smallest. But the rating distributions are lumpy: responses cluster at certain values, and Llama 70B gives mostly very high or very low ratings. No analysis classifies each sample as a 'conditional-probability' or 'conjunction' responder.
numbers: Intraclass correlation over five runs, vanilla, for the P(B|A) task / if-probability / acceptability: Llama 8B .769/.772/.753; Llama 70B .947/.934/.920; Qwen 7B .977/.972/.945; Qwen 72B .969/.967/.978. Few-shot: Llama 8B .793/.754/.760; Llama 70B .944/.956/.882. CoT: Llama 70B .901/.850/.876; Qwen 72B .933/.913/.966.
limits: ICC measures agreement of numbers, not whether samples differ in interpretation style. Gap 10 (style variation across samples) remains untested.
agent_relevance: Number-valued sampling is stable enough to vote on for large models. Style-level voting is still an open test.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis (author copy)
finding: I opened the author copy that the cross-check could not reach. It confirms the reliability numbers: six data sets from the US and Italy where people drew their own conclusions to all 64 premise pairs. Difficulty ranks agree strongly across sets, and hard problems get more varied answers.
numbers: Six experiments, N = 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 56 (total 156): Johnson-Laird and Steedman 1978 Exp 2 (two tests, Columbia), Johnson-Laird and Bara 1984 Exp 3 (Milan), Bara et al. 1995 (two groups, Florence), Roberts et al. 2001 (Florida). Kendall's W = .86 (27 valid items), .64 (37 no-valid-conclusion items), .45 (entropy of responses), all p < .001. Entropy correlates with accuracy at r = -0.52. A response counted as reliable if given in at least 16% of trials (chance 1/9). Seven of the 12 theories were meta-analysed; Euler circles, Venn diagrams, verbal substitution, monotonicity and source-founding were left out.
limits: Samples are small (20 per group) and mostly students. Instruction in these sets was 'what follows with certainty'.
agent_relevance: Closes the paywall gap in the critique for the reliability numbers. Fixed difficulty ranks give a ready calibration table for the agent (S3/S5 effort per problem).

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012), Table 8 (hits, correct rejections, correct predictions)
finding: Confirms the hit and correct-rejection figures quoted by earlier agents. No theory does both well. Mental models predict almost every response people give but also predict many they do not. Illicit conversion does the opposite. Verbal models strike the best balance.
numbers: Hits: mental models 95, verbal models 63, matching 59, PHM 52, atmosphere 51, PSYCOP 44, conversion 44. Correct rejections: conversion 93, verbal models 90, atmosphere 85, PSYCOP 85, PHM 79, mental models 74, matching 74. Correct predictions: verbal models 84, conversion 83, mental models 78, atmosphere 78, PSYCOP 77, PHM 73, matching 71. Aggregates: model-based theories 76, heuristic-based 66. Mental-models hits show publication bias (z = 2.03, p < .05); verbal models marginally heterogeneous (I2 = 52%, Q = 10.69, p = .06). The PDF table is scrambled; I matched rows by the percentages quoted in the text (95/74, 44/93, 63/90, 84).
limits: Scoring counts a theory's predictions against responses given by at least 16% of people; it rewards hits and penalizes over-prediction.
agent_relevance: None of the classic theories is a safe single model for the agent. Use them as error checks (guardrails) rather than as a policy.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012), figural effect on 'nothing follows' and on valid conclusions
finding: Figure affects both which conclusion direction people write and how often they correctly say 'nothing follows'. Valid conclusions that fit the figural bias are drawn about 80% of the time; those that violate it about 20%. The rate of correct 'nothing follows' answers rises with figure number. The authors note that atmosphere and matching cannot explain this.
numbers: Correct 'nothing follows' by figure (mood held constant, data from Johnson-Laird and Bara 1984 Exp 1): Figure 1 50%, Figure 2 57%, Figure 3 70%, Figure 4 86% (Jonckheere z = 3.32, p < .001). Per-item correct 'nothing follows' ranged 15% to 100% in that set. Example: 'All B are A, Some C are B' gets 90% valid answers; 'All B are A, None of the C is B' gets 1%.
quote: When they violate the bias, they are infrequent (around 20%)
limits: The figure numbers come from one study cited in the meta-analysis, not recomputed. The paper reports no separate effect sizes for 'some'-quantifier cases; per-item percentages are in its Table 6.
agent_relevance: If the agent's 'nothing follows' recall also varies with figure, that is a cheap fingerprint of heuristic answering. Add a per-figure breakdown to the 64-mood probe.

source: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012), Table 6 per-syllogism data, recomputed
finding: I recomputed the headline human accuracies from the paper's per-item Table 6. They match the numbers Bertolazzi et al. quote (44.63 valid, 40.97 invalid). The easiest and hardest items are known, and the experimenters' instructions neutralized existential import.
numbers: Mean percent correct over the 27 valid syllogisms: 44.63. Over the 37 no-valid-conclusion syllogisms: 41.05 (unweighted mean of the table's rounded percentages; Bertolazzi quotes 40.97). Easiest valid: 90%; hardest valid: 1%. Easiest invalid: 'None of the A is B, None of the C is B' 76% correct 'nothing follows'; hardest invalid: 'Some of the B are A, All the C are B' 12% (most infer 'Some C are A'). Sample accuracy: selective US university 55% valid; Italian state university 37%.
quote: tell the participants that individuals of all relevant sorts exist
limits: The recomputation is mine, from OCR text of the table. Rounding explains the 0.08 gap on invalid items.
agent_relevance: Gives the human baseline for the agent's 37-item 'nothing follows' recall: about 41% for people, with a wide range by item.

source: Zang et al. (2026) A Syllogistic Probe: Tracing the Evolution of Logic Reasoning in LLMs, Table 3 (closed-source models)
finding: Reasoning-tuned frontier models accept the 15 modern-valid moods and reject the 9 existential-import moods almost perfectly, so they are not averse to saying 'invalid'. GPT-o3 and GPT-5 sit on the modern reading. Non-reasoning and Claude models fall in between or on the traditional side. This is a binary accept/reject task with the conclusion given, so it does not show whether the model would produce 'nothing follows' unprompted.
numbers: Accuracy under the traditional reading (Acct, all 24 moods valid) and the modern reading (Accm). English, non-empty minor term (EN+): GPT-o3 62.50 / 100.00; GPT-5 62.53 / 100.00; Gemini-2.5-Pro 65.17 / 97.33; Gemini-3-Pro-Preview 63.48 / 99.00; Claude-3.7-Sonnet 70.33 / 92.00; Claude-4.5-Sonnet 70.01 / 92.52; GPT-4.1 80.04 / 82.38; GPT-4o 93.33 / 68.75. Recall on invalid (recI) for o3 and GPT-5 about 99.6 to 100. 62.5% = 15/24 moods, so Acct near 62.5 means the model accepts exactly the modern-valid set. With an empty minor term (EN-), Gemini-3-Pro-Preview Acct 98.41 / Accm 64.02.
limits: Validity of a supplied conclusion for one 24-mood template set. No atmosphere-fit score, no production task, no 37-item nothing-follows rate. Per-cell N not extracted.
agent_relevance: For gap 1: frontier reasoning models look different from the 2024 results on rejecting invalid conclusions, but this is not a like-for-like replication of Eisape or Bertolazzi.

source: Zang et al. (2026), Prior-check prompt (Table 4 vs Table 5) and model-family effects
finding: A prompt that first asks 'do you think the major, middle and minor terms are empty sets? keep that in mind and answer' raises modern-logic accuracy for most models without flipping their stance. Qwen3 thinking variants shift to the modern reading faster than same-size instruct models; the Qwen3-30B-A3B thinking variant shifts back toward traditional. CoT on instruct models gives only a partial shift. Stating the existence assumption therefore steers the model, which is what an S0 restatement would do.
numbers: EN+, modern-logic accuracy, baseline to Prior-check: Qwen3-14B-Thinking 87.08 to 97.67; Qwen3-32B-Thinking 77.58 to 87.50; Qwen3-8B-Thinking 75.83 to 78.88; Qwen3-235B-Instruct 97.42 to 99.62; Qwen3-4B 62.67 to 59.71 (down). Modern logic accepts 15 moods, traditional 24. Per-mood consistency of Qwen3-Next-80B Thinking varies from 8.33 to 62.50 across settings, so the stance can be unstable near the transition.
limits: Assignment of captions (Table 4 = Prior-check, Table 5 = baseline) is inferred from caption position in the PDF text. The prompt moves models toward the modern reading; the paper did not test a prompt that pins the traditional reading.
agent_relevance: S0 should state existence assumptions (are the terms non-empty?) and which logic the grader uses. The reverse direction (force the traditional reading) is untested.

source: Valentino, Ranaldi, Pucci, Ranaldi, Freitas (2026) SemEval-2026 Task 11: Disentangling Content and Formal Reasoning in LLMs (task overview)
finding: The shared task benchmark states its reading: the 24 valid Aristotelian schemes 'under Aristotelian interpretation with existential import'. Items come in four quadrants (valid or invalid, plausible or implausible). Systems built as translation plus a deterministic checker or prover dominated, and ten systems reached 100% accuracy with zero content effect on the English validity subtask.
numbers: About 250 participants, over 3000 submissions, 35 system papers. Subtask 1 (English validity): 960 training and 192 test items, equal split over four quadrants. Ten systems at 100 accuracy and 0 content effect, at least seven tagged as pseudo-formal (neuro-symbolic decomposition or prover). Score = Acc / (1 + ln(1 + content effect)). Zero-shot base models: Qwen3 14B 97.38 acc, CE 4.23; Qwen3 8B 95.81, CE 4.23; Llama 3.1 8B 64.17, CE 32.15; Qwen2.5 14B 67.50, CE 44.54. Multilingual subtask 4: best system 90.10 acc.
limits: Items are templated and generated by Gemini 3.0 Pro; the parse is easy, which favors solver pipelines. The task is binary validity of a supplied conclusion. The overview text I read gives no frontier reasoning-model baselines.
agent_relevance: If we benchmark on this set, the correct reading is the traditional one. Note the mismatch with Zang's reasoning models (d12).

source: Kartac, Onderkova, Bronec, Kasner, Lango, Dusek (2026) UFAL-CUNI at SemEval-2026 Task 11: modular neuro-symbolic method
finding: A 4B reasoning LLM that parses each proposition one at a time into first-order logic written as LaTeX (then rewritten by rules to Prover9 syntax) beats the same model judging validity directly. The translation step is where the pipeline works or fails. Existential import needed an explicit patch because Prover9 does not assume it. Many remaining errors were label errors or logic-type ambiguities.
numbers: Validation ablation (Qwen3 4B Thinking, subtask 1): full pipeline 95.83 acc, CE 2.28; direct Prover9 syntax 85.97, CE 12.23 (18% of formulas had syntax errors); LLM as prover over its own FOL 79.22, CE 20.21; end-to-end zero-shot 84.17, CE 14.67; single-step parse 95.81, CE 2.14. Test: 95.29 acc, CE 3.21, rank 19 of 35. Of 21 validation errors, 10 were wrong gold labels and 2 were clear parse errors; 'It is not true that any' read as universal negative caused 5 of the ambiguity errors. The organizers confirmed the existential-import reading; the authors add the particular proposition by regex. Qwen3 4B beat Qwen3 30B-A3B.
limits: Small model, templated data, no token matching to a voting baseline. The paper criticizes the combined-score metric as over-amplifying isolated errors.
agent_relevance: Supports a parse-then-prove step but only with structured intermediate format and an existential-import patch. Report parse error rate separately from reasoning error rate.

source: Advani (2026) lakshadvani at SemEval-2026 Task 11: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Content-Independent Syllogistic Reasoning
finding: A three-way ablation on 960 training items with GPT-5 shows that both a prompt spelling out the rules and a symbolic checker help, with the checker helping most. The model rewrites each sentence with abstract letters A, B, C in one of four standard forms, and a short script looks up the mood and figure among 24 valid forms. Vanilla GPT-5 defaulted to 'invalid': about 60% on valid items, 96% on invalid.
numbers: Vanilla 'is this valid?': 78.1% accuracy, content effect 19.14. Add the 'Logic Compiler' prompt that encodes Aristotelian rules: 89.9%, CE 4.95. Add the symbolic checker: 96.6%, CE 2.63. Competition system (Grok-4.1-fast translation, script check): 100% acc, CE 0 on test subtask 1. Subtask 2 LLM-only system: 95.26% acc, CE 2.94, score 41.08. Direct classification scored 29.20 on subtask 2; telling the model to ignore plausibility 'helped somewhat but TCE stayed high'.
limits: Single author, limited API budget, templated items; the checker needs exactly two premises. Fallback to 'invalid' on any parse failure was a design choice that trades false negatives for lower bias.
agent_relevance: A rules-in-prompt step cuts most of the content effect in a strong model without any solver; a checker removes more. Only partly consistent with K10: a solver as sole judge worked here because the parse is easy.

source: Gupta, Goyal, Bedi (2026) Team 0704mis at SemEval-2026 Task 11: Dual-View Consistency Testing
finding: A multilingual LLM parser extracts the logical form twice, once from the native text and once after content terms are replaced by symbols; a deterministic verifier of the 24 forms decides. Masked parsing alone beat native parsing, so abstraction before parsing helps, but it is paired with a solver.
numbers: Subtask 3, 12 languages: dual-view (official) 95.83% acc, CE 5.21, score 33.91; single-view native 92.08%, CE 4.89, score 29.11; local baseline 68.33%, CE 24.17; single-view masked (post-competition) 97.50%, CE 1.71, score 57.00. Native single view failed to parse 72 cases.
limits: The parser is a Claude Sonnet model (version not stated in the text I read); post-competition results are the team's own. This does not test abstraction followed by free LLM reasoning.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: abstraction helps the parse; it has not been shown to help when the same model then reasons in prose.

source: Rabern, Mondorf, Plank (2026) LogicSkills: A Structured Benchmark for Formal Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Countermodel construction is the hardest of three logical skills for conventional instruction-tuned LLMs and nearly solved by reasoning-tuned ones. Validity-judgment scores can hide the weakness. Fine-tuning on countermodel construction alone did not transfer to validity judgment.
numbers: n = 300 per task and language, first-order two-variable fragment, English and nonce-word versions, solver-verified with Z3. Countermodel accuracy: Llama-3.1-8B 0.00, Llama-3.1-70B 0.12, GPT-4o 0.10, Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.13, DeepSeek-Chat 0.35, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 0.42, Qwen3-32B 0.89, o3 0.99. Conventional models average about 80% on validity, 65% on symbolization, 18% on countermodels. o3: 98.8 validity, 98.7 countermodel, 95.3 symbolization. Of 2020 wrong countermodels, 72.9% were well formed but at least one premise was false. LoRA on Llama-3.2-3B: countermodel 0.0 to 23.0, symbolization 8.3 to 95.0, validity down 15.3 points (format carry-over).
limits: The model is told the argument is invalid and asked to build the countermodel, so the task does not test whether it notices invalidity. Not categorical syllogisms; not prompt-only scaffolds; no equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: For gap 2: no test of an explicit counter-model search step exists, but reasoning-tuned models do this skill natively. A scaffold step for a non-reasoning base is worth a test; for reasoning models it may add tokens without gain.

source: Nguyen, Tachibana, Liu, Liu, Noe, Takeda, Kurohashi (2026) BIS Reasoning 1.0: Japanese Benchmark for Belief-Inconsistent Syllogistic Reasoning
finding: On 5,000 valid but belief-inconsistent syllogisms, reasoning-tuned models are near ceiling and non-reasoning models are not. The reasoning-effort setting matters. For GPT-4o's failures, a CoT prompt or an explicit strict-logic framing recovers most items; plain or casual prompts recover almost none.
numbers: Accuracy (Basic prompt): GPT-5-mini (medium effort) 99.72; GPT-5-nano (medium) 98.84; gpt-oss-20b 98.56; Qwen3-32B without thinking 99.58, with thinking 99.12; GPT-4o 79.54; GPT-5-nano (minimum effort) 69.22; GPT-4-turbo 59.48; Claude-3-Opus 7.18 and Claude-3-Sonnet 20.34 (below chance). On 100 GPT-4o failures re-prompted in English: explicit CoT 87%, strict-logic prompt 76%, polite 65%, basic and casual 3 to 5%.
limits: Only valid items, so it measures acceptance of belief-inconsistent valid conclusions and says nothing about rejecting invalid ones. Japanese; synthetic generation; the prompt comparison was run only on previously failed items (selection effect).
agent_relevance: Content effects on valid items are largely gone for reasoning models; keep content-effect tests on invalid-plausible items too (see Advani). Prompt framing matters for non-reasoning bases.

source: Poddar, Sahoo, Ghosh (2026, AAAI) Understanding Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs from Formal and Natural Language Perspectives, re-read for reasoning models
finding: Re-read with an eye on reasoning-tuned models. Top-tier models have near-perfect syntactic validity accuracy and almost no belief bias, while weaker models and one thinking model (Qwen3-Next 80B Thinking) have large bias. Few-shot lowers accuracy compared with zero-shot.
numbers: 14 LLMs, 4 prompt strategies, 3 temperatures. Belief bias = accuracy on congruent minus incongruent: Gemini 2.5 Flash +0.9 (100.0 vs 99.2), Gemini 2.5 Pro +1.4, GLM-4.6 +1.9, Kimi-K2 +7.5, DeepSeek V3.1 +7.9, Gemini Flash Lite +12.5, Qwen3-Next 80B Thinking +28.0 (86.3 vs 58.3), Llama 3.3 70B +31.6, Llama 3.2 3B +46.9. Top-tier syntactic accuracy 99.6%. Few-shot mean 79.1 vs zero-shot 82.7 (t41 = 2.50, p = 0.0165).
limits: Binary 'does the conclusion follow' task; no 'produce a conclusion' format, so it cannot show whether 'nothing follows' is given spontaneously. Only Table 4 bias values and the text are cited; syntactic accuracy per model was read from a heatmap and not used.
agent_relevance: Content effects on a binary validity task can vanish in current strong models. Treat this as model-dependent, not as a property of 'reasoning' in general.

source: Ando and Mineshima (2026) Do Diagrams Help Large Language Models Reason? Evidence from Syllogistic Reasoning
finding: Even a strong non-reasoning model answers 'neutral' (neither entailed nor contradicted, the closest analogue of 'nothing follows') much less often than it should, and the weaker model nearly never. Added logic notation, linear diagrams or Euler diagrams do not reliably help.
numbers: 285 problems, labels only (no CoT). Claude 3.5 Sonnet, natural language: overall 84.6; entailment 97.9; contradiction 92.6; neutral 63.2. GPT-4o-mini: overall 68.8; entailment 81.1; contradiction 100.0; neutral 25.3. Euler-diagram condition: 84.2 and 67.0 overall; linear diagram 81.1 and 64.9. Conversion cases in NL: Claude 84.2; GPT-4o-mini 52.6 (36.8 with Euler). GPT-4o-mini NL accuracy by figure: F1 89.1, F2 66.7, F3 69.5, F4 58.7.
limits: Direct answer without reasoning. Older multimodal models; no reasoning model. Neutral is not the same as 'no conclusion linking the end terms'.
agent_relevance: Confirms the 'avoids nothing follows' pattern for non-reasoning models and shows a figural gradient (F4 worst). The effect of forcing a neutral check is untested.

source: Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Abe, Mineshima, Okada (2024) Exploring Reasoning Biases in LLMs Through Syllogism: NeuBAROCO, Translate-and-Explain results
finding: Asking GPT-4 to first translate premises into predicate logic and then explain raised accuracy a little in English and Japanese. It did not help GPT-3.5, which translated well in English but then reasoned worse. The model often says 'contradiction' when the right answer is 'neither', and its neutral accuracy is about 30 points below the other labels.
numbers: 90 problems, one-shot structured prompt. Answer accuracy: GPT-4 English: explanation only 77.78; predicate-logic translation 83.33 (translation correct 96.67%, 87/90); set-theory translation 80.00 (translation correct 92.22%). GPT-4 Japanese: 70.00; 75.56 (translation 95.56%); 74.44. GPT-3.5 English: 58.89; 52.22 (translation 91.11%); 54.44. source: Parmar et al. (2024) LogicBench: Towards Systematic Evaluation of Logical Reasoning Ability of LLMs
finding: Modus tollens is among the weakest rules for several models in propositional logic, and the authors link this to negation embedded in rules. The pattern is not simply 'MT is hard': in first-order MT items the models accept readily but reject poorly.

First-order MT 'yes' accuracy 88 to 93 and 'no' accuracy 62 to 77 for four of five models (GPT-4's 'yes' value is garbled in the PDF text).

source: Akinfaderin and Diallo (2026) FregeLogic at SemEval-2026 Task 11 (cost and prompt appendix)
finding: The vote-then-solve system makes six LLM calls and one Z3 solve per item, about 4,300 tokens each. Prompt style matters for content effect: chain-of-thought lowers it for some models and raises it for others, so CoT is not a reliable debiasing step.
numbers: N = 960, nested 5-fold. Cost 4,300 tokens and 12.1 s sequential latency per instance (2.8 s parallel). GPT-OSS-20B: zero-shot 79.0% acc, CE 13.67; simple CoT 65.5%, CE 31.14; few-shot CoT 73.0%, CE 18.92. GPT-OSS-120B: zero-shot 80.0, CE 15.71; simple CoT 75.5, CE 19.88. Llama 4 Maverick few-shot CoT raises CE from 3.83 (plain few-shot) to 10.11. Qwen with CoT 88.0, CE 5.07 (zero-shot 80.5, CE 8.86). Simple CoT had the lowest mean CE (5.24) across the three open models. 11 wrong Z3 flips, all from extraction errors; extraction failure 0.0% in three quadrants and 0.4% in valid-unbelievable.
limits: No single-model run at the same token budget as the ensemble, so the equal-token comparison (gap 7) is still missing. Models are open and small to mid-size.
agent_relevance: Supports the design rule of calling a solver only when votes split. Needs a matched-token comparison against 5-sample voting without a solver and against one long reasoning run.
